Don't make this a Yv4-specific change.  If we should do a lazy-remount instead of an unmount, propose that in the common file.

- I don't think there is any need to remount the file-system to read-only before execute the sled power cycle.

- BusyBox’s mount implementation simply doesn’t provide any lazy remount option.

I think Patrick's recommendation is to move this to some place common so we can ensure all platform's sled-cycle handlers initiate this (at the minimum).
But I am ok with this change going into Y4 before being refactored into common.

Why wouldn't we try a readonly remount first and if that fails then do a lazy unmount?

Doesn't an unmount potentially cause issues where daemons can no longer write to regions of the flash they expected to?  Why is a lazy unmount explicitly better than a readonly remount?  Is there such a thing as a "lazy remount"?

Firstly, remounting the persist filesystem as read-only actually increases the likelihood of flash memory corruption on our Yosemite4 system, as mentioned in the commit message.

Could I ask what issue the remount is intended to address, and why you prefer to keep it? I think we need to be aligned on these points before we can properly discuss this patch.

> Firstly, remounting the persist filesystem as read-only actually increases the likelihood of flash memory corruption on our Yosemite4 system, as mentioned in the commit message.

The commit message had a pretty weak assertion:
    Testing indicates it can even increase the likelihood of corruption.

Do you have data to back this up?  What is the probability of corruption with a read-only remount and a probability of corruption without a read-only remount?

Intuitively, I have no idea why a read-only remount would make corruption _more likely_ than doing nothing.  In practice, maybe your data is correct, but I just have no idea why that would be the case.  Do you have any ideas why?

> Could I ask what issue the remount is intended to address, and why you prefer to keep it? I think we need to be aligned on these points before we can properly discuss this patch.

As I mentioned on Discord, the contributor claimed that they saw better corruption numbers.  I similarly didn't press them on it because it seemed intuitive that it _might_ be better and at least _shouldn't_ be worse.
Hi @patrick@stwcx.xyz, the read-only remount actually performed worse in our tests. You can check the ticket I mentioned on Discord.
Hi @patrick@stwcx.xyz, just checking if there’s any update on your side. Thanks.

Hi @patrick@stwcx.xyz ,

We use Ftrace(kprobe) to trace the underlying UBIFS operation “mount -o remount,ro /run/mnt-persist” while continuously writing to OverlayFS.

Since the observed incidence of UBIFS corruption leading to factory resets is only 1.05% during testing, we implemented a background script to increase the reproducibility. This script continuously performs file copy operations to directories mounted via OverlayFS (/etc and /var) to stress the file system.

When UBIFS is remounted as read-only, it triggers a commit operation to persist 
all in-memory metadata (TNC, LPT) to Flash.

However, if file descriptors remain open during the remount process, VFS continues 
flushing dirty pages into the UBIFS journal. This creates a race condition:

The commit writes a Master Node pointing to a specific version of the LPT (LEB Properties Table).
Simultaneously, new journal entries are written to LEBs whose properties may not match what the LPT recorded.
Upon the next boot, UBIFS recovery attempts to replay the journal using the LPT referenced by the Master Node. If the LPT indicates a LEB should contain index nodes, but the journal actually wrote data nodes there, UBIFS detects this inconsistency and reports a corrupted file system.

The fact that corruption still occurs even after waiting several minutes post-remount confirms that the inconsistent state was already persisted to Flash at the moment of remount — no amount of waiting afterward can fix it.

And we notice UBIFS driver's ubifs_remount_ro 
function assumes that the VFS has 
already stopped all write operations.
( https://github.com/AspeedTech-BMC/linux/blob/0364b2fdf854b9f3c23752d2d499747f342f42e4/fs/ubifs/super.c#L1884 )

But in the real case, some system services still attempt to write data to UBIFS via VFS. (bmcweb.service, rsyslog.service, systemd-journald.service)
Acknowledged. Thanks a lot for the detailed explanation and the experiments.
